overview: The atlas calls this peninsula-shaped layer “Paleo-Koreans,” but archaeologists did not uncover a people using that label. From 1500 to 500 BCE, its unchanged border covers much of inland Korea from near Pyeongyang to Gyeongju, yet leaves out Jeju, Busan, northeastern Korea and Liaodong. Inside and beyond that drawing, localized Mumun communities farmed rice, foxtail millet, broomcorn millet, beans and wheat; gathered wild foods; lived in earth-cut houses; spun fibers; shaped plain and red-polished pottery; and harvested grain with stone knives looped to the hand. Children learned these skills beside experienced workers, although no schoolroom or lesson text survives. Villages stored food, shared labor and sometimes raised enormous dolmen capstones. Rare bronze daggers and ornaments marked connections and status, while most everyday work still relied on stone, wood and clay. Human bones and isotope chemistry reveal diet and health only in small samples. Archaeologists have identified no certain toilet, so the honest bathroom fact is a blank space, not a funny invention. No writing securely belongs to this layer either. Later Korean languages, Gojoseon stories and states require separate evidence. When the map color ends, farms, families, craft and exchange continue; an editorial category disappears, not its people.

periods.title: A map label begins as Mumun lifeways spread
periods.summary: The atlas replaces its broader Koreans layer with a smaller Paleo-Koreans polygon. Archaeological chronologies place new plain pottery, agricultural settlements and polished farming tools around this transition, but they do not identify one ethnicity or spoken language.

periods.title: Early farming evidence grows, unevenly
periods.summary: Charred seeds, field traces and radiocarbon dates show cultivation expanding through varied peninsula environments. The evidence comes from particular excavated contexts; a crop’s arrival cannot by itself prove mass migration, political unity, or a named population.

periods.title: New households and toolkits appear
periods.summary: Many researchers date especially sharp changes in dwellings, pottery, polished stone tools and crop use near 1300 BCE. Competing language-dispersal models remain hypotheses because pots and rice preserve differently from speech, which leaves no direct archaeological fossil.

periods.title: Settled farming does not tell a simple population story
periods.summary: Radiocarbon-date distributions suggest population changed around food-production transitions, yet intensive rice farming did not simply begin because numbers were already soaring. Taphonomy, excavation intensity and calibration all complicate using dated samples as a head count.

periods.title: Fields preserve daily work better than royal names
periods.summary: At Pyeonggeo-dong, AMS dates, sediments, field layouts and crop remains let researchers rebuild repeated agricultural use. This is excellent evidence for labor and land management, but it does not supply the inhabitants’ autonym, ruler, language, or borders.

periods.title: Households cooperate while storing differently
periods.summary: Settlement comparison finds relatively low inequality in house size alongside stronger variation in pottery and storage. Communities could coordinate work while households pursued different advantages; neither perfect equality nor centralized rule follows automatically from a large village.

periods.title: Aggregation and paddy labor reshape some regions
periods.summary: In southeastern settlements, researchers test whether wet-field rice labor helped people cluster into larger communities. Other districts kept different field systems and settlement paths, so no single southern sequence should be stretched across the atlas polygon.

periods.title: Songguk-ri networks become prominent
periods.summary: Rice, storage, distinctive houses, burials and rare prestige objects make Songguk-ri and related sites central to this phase. Plant remains suggest rice was community food rather than an elite monopoly, while regional crop mixtures remained diverse.

periods.title: Large settlements, status and environmental stress coexist
periods.summary: Some communities aggregated, invested in monuments and used rare bronzes while climate archives register changing monsoon, vegetation and fire conditions. Correlation is not proof that weather caused settlement change; social choices, conflict and research visibility also matter.

periods.title: Bronze networks grow as the atlas category nears its end
periods.summary: Liaoning-style daggers, ornaments and regional craft differences reveal exchange and emerging status, but stone tools stayed central. Scholars debate cultural relationships, and artifact similarities cannot name every maker Korean, Gojoseon, Yemaek or any other later ethnonym.

items.text: The live record is exactly Paleo-Koreans, classified as an approximate culture from 1500 to 500 BCE. It has three observed border intervals and no reviewed card. Those database fields describe an editorial map layer; they are not an ancient census, self-name, language label or state archive.

Every exact snapshot contains the same single polygon: one part, one ring, eighty-three positions and bounds about 124.41 to 129.47° east by 34.27 to 40.30° north. Identical geometry across a millennium is a cartographic simplification, not proof that communities or influence stood still.

Audited points near Pyeongyang, Seoul, Chuncheon, Wonju, Daejeon, Jeonju, Daegu and Gyeongju fall inside. Busan, Jeju, Chongjin, Rason, Dandong, Shenyang and northern Kyushu do not. The label therefore cannot represent every prehistoric community on the peninsula or every later Korean homeland.

At 2000 BCE the atlas calls a much larger peninsula-and-Manchuria region Koreans. At 1500 BCE it switches to Paleo-Koreans while assigning Liaodong to Sinic. That rename and contraction are map-editor choices; archaeology does not document a matching five-hundred-year ethnic costume change.

The target vanishes at 500 BCE, leaving audited Korean points blank; Gojoseon appears only in the 400 BCE file with a different polygon extending into Liaodong. A hundred-year gap and changed geometry make automatic direct predecessor or successor claims irresponsible.

Archaeologists combine stratigraphy, artifact associations, calibrated radiocarbon dates and charred plant remains. Flotation makes burned seeds rise for collection; direct dating can test pottery-based timelines. Each method has error ranges, so “about 900 BCE” is more honest than pretending every house began in one exact year.

Songguk-ri has been investigated through twenty-five excavation campaigns. Researchers documented houses, pits, post-built structures, fences, graves, tools, pottery and crops across only part of a huge protected site. Its importance comes from layered evidence, while incomplete excavation warns against reconstructing a whole society from one trench.

Jungdo’s immense dwelling record helps study settlement aggregation, but radiocarbon and bootstrap research warns that pottery styles are imperfect clocks. Houses found together were not necessarily occupied together; a busy-looking plan may compress generations of building, repair, abandonment and rebuilding onto one page.

Portable X-ray fluorescence measures elements in pottery without cutting a sample, helping test whether vessels share clay recipes or production zones. Scientific readings complement shape and decoration; they cannot reveal a potter’s ethnicity, spoken language, personal name or political loyalty.

Acidic soils often destroy bone and other organic material, so health and diet datasets remain small. Compound-specific carbon and nitrogen isotopes can separate millet, rice, terrestrial protein and aquatic signals, but results describe sampled people at dated sites rather than everyone inside the atlas boundary.

Human bone chemistry from central inland Mumun burials shows substantial consumption of C4 plants, most plausibly foxtail and broomcorn millet. This corrects a rice-only picture. Diet differed by region, and seven sampled people cannot serve as a menu for millions of lives across a thousand years.

At Sangdong-dong and Songguk-ri, crop remains indicate rice was eaten within farming communities rather than reserved only for elites. That conclusion concerns these early first-millennium BCE assemblages; later taxation and prestige histories should not be projected backward into every Mumun household.

Semi-lunar stone knives had holes for a cord loop around the hand, letting harvesters cut grain ears. Their shapes included crescent, square, trapezoid, pear, fish and triangle. Fun fact: the ancient “moon knife” family included several tools that looked nothing like a moon.

At Nukdo, carbon and nitrogen isotopes test how terrestrial mammals, plants and seafood contributed near the late Mumun boundary. Coastal shell middens remind us that agriculture and marine foods could coexist. Results from this island setting are comparison, not a universal peninsula-wide diet.

Early longhouses commonly kept storage pits indoors; later settlements sometimes separated houses, storage and ritual areas. Stored grain represented months of labor and future meals, making access socially important. Archaeological pits show capacity and placement, but seldom identify exactly who held the key or distributed shares.

sections.title: Homes, water and the bathroom mystery

items.text: Early Mumun homes were often long rectangular pit houses with several hearths; some exceeded one hundred square metres. Archaeologists cautiously suggest multiple domestic groups may have shared large buildings. House size gives clues about co-residence, but it cannot by itself prove a particular family tree or marriage rule.

Middle Mumun regions developed smaller round or square houses alongside raised-floor and post-built structures. At Songguk-ri, hearths, central pits, posts and activity areas varied by building. Earth-cut floors offered shelter, while roofs and walls of perishable materials survive mostly as stains and holes.

Villages favored access to streams, fields and manageable slopes, and some excavations reveal ditches or reservoirs linked to farming. Water supported people, crops and craft, but published features should not be relabeled as drinking pipes. No evidence supports household taps, sewers or a standardized water authority.

No toilet structure has been conclusively identified from Korea’s Bronze Age. Researchers may test soil, parasite eggs and waste deposits, yet later cesspits and flush systems cannot be copied backward. So the responsible toilet reconstruction is simple: arrangements are unknown, and guesses need labels.

Pits, ditches, burned soil, broken pots and plant remains can represent storage, work, disposal, accidents or later disturbance. Context decides. Ancient rubbish is archaeological treasure, but calling every pit a trash can, or every ditch a drain, would turn a careful excavation into a guessing game.

Comparing seventy-three settlements, researchers find low inequality in house size but more variation in pottery holdings. This suggests cooperation and competition could coexist. It does not prove that everyone had equal power, and rare prestige graves show that status could be expressed outside ordinary household floors.

Gender is hard to reconstruct because graves preserve unevenly and archaeologists historically asked too few questions about women. A specialist review warns against making women invisible or assigning every weapon to a man and every spindle to a woman. Tasks and identities require evidence, not stereotypes.

The small Bronze Age skeletal record includes adults and children, but preservation and excavation are uneven. Bones can estimate age, biological traits, diet and disease cautiously; they cannot supply modern ethnic identity. Genetic or physical resemblance must never be used to rename a whole archaeological culture.

No school building, alphabet lesson or named teacher survives. Children nevertheless had to learn planting, harvesting, fire care, pottery handling, spinning and safe tool use. Spindle whorls and weights show repeated skilled production; describing learning by observation and practice is plausible, while formal classes are unsupported.

Early longhouses with multiple hearths may have held several domestic groups; smaller Middle Mumun houses imply changing household organization. Researchers discuss kin connections across nearby dwellings, but exact descent, residence and marriage rules remain unknown. Modern Korean family customs cannot fill that prehistoric silence.

Spindle whorls and loom-related weights occur widely at Early and Middle Mumun sites, supporting fiber spinning and weaving. Actual cloth rarely survives, so fiber species, colors, cuts and who wore what remain uncertain. A whorl proves thread-making technology, not a fully reconstructed prehistoric wardrobe.

Plain coarse pottery was shaped for cooking and storage, while red-burnished vessels received extra finishing. Metric research suggests much ordinary pottery was household or village production, but red-burnished wares circulated more widely through skilled production. “Plain” therefore describes decoration, not careless workmanship.

Quartz and other stones became axes, adzes, daggers, arrowheads, sickles, knives, grinders and harvesting tools. Chuncheon museum finds even preserve rare willow arrow shafts. Organic handles usually vanish, so a bare museum blade is only part of the tool its maker intended.

Early bronze was rare; everyday cutting, farming and woodworking remained dominated by stone and wood. The national museum notes no peninsula tin deposits and no clear Bronze Age copper-smelting proof, so found bronzes may reflect complex exchange, remelting or production histories rather than simple local mines.

Portable X-ray fluorescence can compare elemental signatures in pots, while typology compares rim, body and surface treatment. Combining laboratory and visual methods helps identify technological traditions. Neither technique reads personal intention perfectly, and both depend on secure excavation context and appropriate comparative samples.

Liaoning-type bronze daggers have a curved, lute-like blade and detachable hilt. Examples connect the peninsula with northeastern China between roughly 1000 and 400 BCE. Similar weapons show movement of objects and ideas; they do not prove a single empire, ethnicity or language stretched across every findspot.

Bronze axes, chisels, daggers, mirrors and ritual objects coexisted with stone tools. Regional assemblages differ enough that a National Museum review rejects easy identification with one named tribe. Archaeological “cultures” organize material patterns; they are analytical tools, not recovered passports.

Fine-line mirrors required controlled alloying, molds, casting and finishing. Their gleam and burial context support ritual or authority interpretations near the later Bronze Age, but mirrors this elaborate cluster around or after the card’s final centuries. They should illuminate continuity, not decorate every earlier household.

Millet, rice and associated technologies moved through East Asia in discontinuous steps. Crop dates can trace cultivation pathways, yet seeds do not speak. Farming packages could spread through migration, exchange, imitation, intermarriage or several processes together, none automatically equivalent to Korean ethnicity.

Attached-rim pottery and changing artifact associations become important around the later endpoint and beyond. Careful typology shows sequence and interaction in Seoul and Gyeonggi, but the forms overlap transitions. A neat 500 BCE map cutoff should not be mistaken for every potter changing style overnight.

sections.title: Health, care and medicine without make-believe

items.text: Porous bone, joint change, teeth and healed injury can preserve episodes of stress or survival, but Korea’s Bronze Age skeletal sample is small. Researchers need sex, age, burial context, preservation and comparison before diagnosis. One skeleton’s condition is a life story, never a population-wide medical chart.

Isotope chemistry shows what kinds of foods supplied protein and carbon over years, not last night’s dinner. Central Mumun samples point strongly toward millet, while other sites differ. Nutrition, status, season and ecology remain entangled, and healthy-looking chemistry does not identify medicines or caregivers.

No securely dated medical text, pharmacy or named healer survives from this layer. People surely responded to cuts, burns, childbirth, aching joints and illness, but specific herbs, surgeries or theories cannot be asserted without evidence. Care may be inferred only where survival or treatment traces support it.

Denser farming settlements brought people, waste, stored food and water into closer contact. That could change disease risks, but direct parasite evidence from this period is scarce and no certain toilet is known. Later Korean sanitation archaeology provides methods for investigation, not a Bronze Age answer.

Archaeobotany recovers foods that could support health, while bones record only some stresses. Researchers cannot translate soybeans, azuki beans, grains and gathered nuts into a complete nutrition score because recipes, portions, age, season and access vary. The safest conclusion is diverse food potential alongside substantial local difference.

Hundreds of dolmens at Gochang, Hwasun and Ganghwa preserve chambers, capstones, quarry evidence and changing forms. Moving stones weighing many tons demanded planning and labor. The monuments reveal commemoration and social action, but no surviving prayer tells us what builders called ancestors or the afterlife.

Chuncheon dolmens include collapsed chambers, moved stones, pottery and a stone harvesting knife. Such details show why excavation matters: a restored capstone alone cannot explain sequence or contents. Researchers document displacement and disturbance before using a monument to infer ceremony, rank or community labor.

Songguk-ri graves contained stone cists, pits and jars, with rare daggers, arrowheads, ornaments and red pottery in selected burials. Unequal goods suggest status distinctions, yet a rich grave does not automatically identify a king, priest or man. Burial performance and everyday power need not match perfectly.

Palisades, deep ditches, burned houses, polished daggers and arrowheads may signal defense or organized violence. Each clue has alternatives: fire can be accidental, ditches can organize space, and weapons can be ritual. Conflict is plausible in some places, but a peninsula-wide war is unsupported.

Bronze mirrors may have reflected sunlight or sounded in ritual, while rare daggers embodied authority. These interpretations fit special burial sets and technical investment; they remain interpretations. No inscription names a deity, office or ceremony, so later shamanic titles and national myths should stay outside this card.

Mumun communities coordinated fields, maintained settlements, stored harvests, spun fibers, made durable pottery and polished specialized stone tools. These were major technical and social achievements even when bronze stayed rare. Calling the era Bronze Age must not make farmers’ stone, wood, soil and plant knowledge seem secondary.

Dolmen building joined quarry knowledge, transport, leverage, scheduling and shared labor. Large villages likewise required negotiation around fields, paths, storage and fire. Monumental success did not require a modern state, and cooperation should not be mistaken automatically for forced labor or absolute chiefly command.

Written-language sample: none. No securely attributable text, script or language survives from this exact atlas record between 1500 and 500 BCE. Old Korean evidence is much later and fragmentary; borrowing Hangul, Three Kingdoms inscriptions or reconstructed Proto-Koreanic would manufacture an ancient voice.

Idu used Chinese characters to represent Korean grammar and sounds, but surviving examples belong to the Three Kingdoms and later periods, many centuries after this card. Even the modern written form 무문토기, “Mumun pottery,” is a scholarly label, not a prehistoric inscription or sample.

At 500 BCE the atlas polygon disappears, but archaeology does not show farms, households or craft vanishing on command. Later pottery, bronze and eventually iron traditions developed through regional change. The map’s blank seam and 400 BCE Gojoseon layer must remain editorial transitions, not an invented conquest.

ending.text: At about 500 BCE the exact Paleo-Koreans id disappears, while audited peninsula points have no owner in that snapshot. Gojoseon appears only at 400 BCE across changed geometry that includes Liaodong. Neither the blank century nor the later label proves collapse, conquest or ethnic replacement. Mumun-period farms, households, monuments, craft and exchange followed varied regional paths into later bronze and iron-using communities. Because the atlas supplies no securely supported historical successor, this card ends with continuity and leaves predecessor and successor arrays empty.
